analysis.one_liner: Required rerouting of dangerous toxic chemical rail shipments away from major cities, with training grants, whistleblower protections, and million-dollar penalties.
analysis.headline: The bill was referred to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced in June 2005, never received a hearing, markup, or vote, and died when the 109th Congress ended in January 2007 with zero cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill directed the Homeland Security Department to write rules for shipping and storing extremely hazardous materials — things like chlorine and other toxic-by-inhalation gases — by rail. The core rule: these shipments would have to be routed around designated "high threat corridors," meaning dense population centers and high-risk areas, with narrow exceptions. Railroads would have had to tell governors, mayors, and local emergency responders what was moving through their communities, employees who report violations would be protected from retaliation, state and local governments could sue violators, and penalties could reach $1 million per violation. It also authorized about $100 million in safety-training grants and $10 million a year to train rail hazmat workers through labor organizations. It was introduced by Senator Biden with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Commerce Committee on the day it arrived, and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Residents of major cities and other areas that railroads route toxic chemical trains through would have gained the most: the bill's findings cite federal estimates that a successful attack on a single 90-ton toxic-gas tanker in a dense area could kill or injure up to 100,000 people, and rerouting was designed to move that risk away from population centers [S3]. City officials and first responders would have gained advance knowledge of what hazardous materials move through their communities, plus grants for training and equipment [S2, S3]. Railroad workers would have gained federal hazmat training programs and legal protection against being fired for reporting safety violations [S3].
analysis.who_benefits_short: City residents near toxic rail lines

how_it_helps.text: It required rerouting shipments of extremely hazardous materials around designated 'high threat corridors' — dense population centers and national-security areas — so fewer people would be exposed if a tanker were attacked or ruptured [S3].

It required railroads to tell governors, mayors, and local emergency responders what quantities and types of hazardous materials pass through or are stored in their communities, and to file risk-management plans [S3].
It protected railroad employees from being fired or punished for reporting violations to federal agencies, enforceable through a lawsuit for reinstatement and damages [S3].
It authorized $100 million in training grants for local governments and railroads, plus $10 million a year to train rail hazmat workers through nonprofit employee organizations [S2, S3].
It let state and local governments sue violators and imposed penalties of up to $1 million per violation, giving cities a way to enforce the rules themselves [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Freight railroads and chemical shippers would have borne the cost. The bill's own findings state that the principal cost of rerouting is the additional operating expense of longer hauls, and shippers would have faced reporting duties, whistleblower liability, civil suits from state and local governments, and administrative penalties of up to $1 million per violation [S2, S3]. Some of those costs would likely have been passed through to the prices of goods shipped by rail.

drawbacks.text: The bill's own findings acknowledge that rerouting toxic shipments is the most expensive part of the approach: the principal cost is the added operating expense of longer hauls, which railroads and chemical shippers would have borne and eventually passed on [S3].

The re-routing mandate was broad: it covered toxic-by-inhalation gases, explosives, flammable gases, and even high-level nuclear waste, with exceptions left largely to the discretion of the Homeland Security Secretary, which risked inconsistent or politicized decisions about which cities got protection [S3].

A 90-day deadline for the Secretary to issue complex routing and storage regulations was unrealistic and could have produced rushed rules, and penalties of up to $1 million per failure applied without a graduated scale for smaller violations [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main cost was real: rerouting toxic shipments around cities adds miles, fuel, and operating expense for railroads and chemical shippers, and some shipments might have qualified for exceptions anyway. The main benefit was also real: the bill's own findings cite federal studies of toxic plumes capable of killing or injuring tens of thousands if a tanker were attacked in a dense area, so moving those tankers away from population centers addresses a catastrophic, if low-probability, risk, and the whistleblower and notification provisions gave local officials and workers tools they did not otherwise have. On balance the bill targeted a genuine vulnerability, but as introduced it was one-sided against shippers on cost and it never received a hearing where those tradeoffs could be worked out.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the Senate Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, the committee never took it up, and it expired when the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Biden introduced the bill on June 16, 2005 and gave introductory remarks the same day [S5].
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation — the standard first step for a Senate bill [S5].
No senator signed on as a cosponsor [S4].
The action history shows no hearing, no markup, no committee vote, and no floor action for the rest of the 109th Congress; the last entry is the June 16, 2005 referral [S5].
The bill died automatically on January 3, 2007, when the 109th Congress ended and all unpassed bills expired [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Freight railroads and chemical shippers are better off: they avoided rerouting costs, new reporting duties, and million-dollar penalties, while keeping the right to route toxic tank cars through major cities as before.

for.name: Sen. Joseph R. Biden, Jr.
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on June 16, 2005 and delivered introductory remarks on the Senate floor [S1, S5].

against.name: Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 16, 2005 and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress — no hearing, markup, or vote [S5].

against.name: Freight railroads and chemical shippers
against.what_they_did: The bill would have imposed rerouting costs and penalties on them; mandatory rerouting of toxic chemical trains was contested industry-wide during this period.

against.name: The Senate as a whole
against.what_they_did: No senator cosponsored the bill, leaving it with no visible support beyond its author [S4].

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever taken and no senator cosponsored the bill, so the record shows only a Democratic sponsor and no measurable support from either party.

industries.note: The bill would have forced them to reroute toxic shipments around major cities, report movements to federal and local officials, and face up to $1 million in penalties per violation. Its death meant they kept their existing routing, including through dense downtown areas, at no added operating cost.

Rerouting mandates and civil suits by state and local governments would have raised the cost of shipping chlorine and other toxic chemicals and created new legal exposure. The bill never advanced, so those costs never materialized.

industries.industry: Rail hazmat workers and first responders
industries.note: Workers would have gained $10 million a year in federally funded hazmat training and new whistleblower protections; first responders would have gained $100 million in training and equipment grants plus advance notice of what was moving through their communities. They got none of it.

Cities gained a right to petition for 'high threat corridor' designation, advance disclosure of hazardous shipments, and standing to sue violators in federal court. The bill's failure left them relying on voluntary railroad cooperation.
